analysis.one_liner: Suspends nearly all costly new federal regulations for one year.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 25 Senate Republicans plus its sponsor, never received a committee vote or hearing before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would freeze for one year virtually every major final federal regulation that had not yet taken effect as of September 2011 — rules covering the environment, public health, workplace safety, and finance — unless an agency head personally exempted it. The stated goal was to reduce costs on businesses during a weak job market. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee and died there without a vote, a hearing, or any further action for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that would have had to comply with upcoming federal rules — from financial institutions implementing the 2010 Wall Street reform law to power plants, chemical facilities, and manufacturers facing new environmental and safety requirements — would have gained a year without compliance costs. Industry groups at the time widely argued that pending rules were suppressing hiring.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would block any final regulation taking effect after September 1, 2011 that raises business costs and is likely to have a $100 million annual economic effect or otherwise materially affect the economy, jobs, environment, or public health, for a full year after enactment.
Rules that had already taken effect would be treated as though they never took effect during the freeze year, suspending compliance obligations retroactively.

Agency heads could exempt rules they found necessary for imminent threats to health or safety, criminal enforcement, job creation, economic growth, military or foreign affairs, or tax administration — but the exemption criteria for 'job creation' and 'economic growth' were subjective and self-determined.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through delayed protections: air and water safeguards, workplace and product safety rules, and Wall Street reform rules implementing the 2010 Dodd-Frank law would all be held back for a year, while the harms those rules address continued. Taxpayers and communities would absorb any resulting pollution, fraud, or safety incidents during the pause.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers, consumers, and communities awaiting protections

drawbacks.text: The freeze was not targeted: it would delay all major new rules across health, safety, environment, and finance for a year, including rules finished and vetted through years of public comment, and would retroactively nullify rules already in effect, upending compliance plans and leaving regulated parties in legal limbo.

The exemption process concentrated sweeping, subjective discretion in individual agency heads — a rule could escape the freeze simply if its 'principal effect' were 'encouraging economic growth' — which critics could view as either a safety valve or an unaccountable loophole.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that many of the pending rules addressed concrete hazards — including rules required by the Dodd-Frank financial reform enacted after the 2008 crisis — and that a blanket pause trades a year of those protections for uncertain and unquantified job gains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered businesses a one-year compliance holiday on new rules during a sluggish 2011 economy. Against that, it would have suspended, across the board, environmental, health, safety, and financial rules — many years in the making and some mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank reform — and would have retroactively canceled rules already in effect. The one-year delay limited the harm, but the design was a blunt freeze rather than a review of specific burdensome rules, and the cost would fall on the people those rules protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Susan Collins introduced the bill on September 12, 2011, joined by 17 original Republican cosponsors listed on the bill text.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs on the day of introduction; that referral was the last action ever taken on it.
The bill accumulated 25 cosponsors, all Republicans, and never received a committee vote, hearing, or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, no one gained from it directly. The people protected by pending environmental, health, safety, and financial rules kept those protections on their original schedule, while regulated industries received no pause in their compliance obligations.

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 25 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat or independent supported the bill, and the Senate committee chaired by the Democratic caucus never took it up.

industries.industry: Businesses facing new federal regulations (manufacturers, energy and chemical facilities, financial firms)
industries.note: The bill would give them a one-year exemption from compliance with major new rules, shifting the cost of pollution, fraud, and safety hazards onto workers, consumers, and communities.

industries.industry: Federal rule-writing agencies and the rulemaking process
industries.note: A blanket one-year suspension would stall the government's ability to issue and enforce major rules, including rules already finalized after years of public input, and retroactively nullify ones in effect.
